blocks.text: 1. Drift Detection
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444503135-589871391.png

Monitoring, the previous topic, introduced data health checks as an informal comparison between live incoming data and the training data's known shape. Drift Detection formalizes that informal check into a rigorous, statistical comparison instead.

The core question drift detection answers is whether the live data distribution is genuinely, statistically different from the training data distribution, not just superficially different by chance. This gives a considerably more precise, defensible answer than a simple average-value comparison alone, the kind covered in the Monitoring topic's worked example, can actually provide.
2. Two Genuinely Distinct Kinds of Drift

blocks.alt: Two Genuinely Distinct Kinds of Drift
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444503136-59583607.png

Data drift, also called covariate shift, describes a situation where the input features' distribution changes over time, but the true underlying relationship between those features and the target stays exactly the same. Concept drift describes something genuinely different: the actual relationship between inputs and the target itself changes over time.

This distinction matters enormously for deciding what to actually do once drift is detected, a distinction covered in full at the end of this topic. Confusing the two, treating a genuine concept drift as if it were merely harmless data drift, is a real, consequential mistake.

blocks.text: 3. An Example of Data Drift
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444503136-292026737.png

Consider a house-price model trained mostly on data describing smaller homes. Over time, suppose the real estate market genuinely shifts, and larger homes start being listed more frequently than they were during the training period.

Square footage's distribution has shifted meaningfully, more large values now appear than the model ever saw much of during training, but the underlying truth that a bigger house genuinely predicts a higher price has not changed at all. This is a textbook case of pure data drift, the input population changed, the relationship itself did not.
4. An Example of Concept Drift
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444503136-965292656.png

Consider instead a fraud detection model trained before some genuinely new fraud pattern emerged in the wild. Fraudsters change tactics over time, and if they adopt an entirely new approach, the old warning signs the model originally learned to recognize may simply no longer apply.

Here, the relationship between features and the actual fraud label has genuinely, meaningfully changed, the exact same feature values that once reliably indicated legitimate activity might now indicate fraud, or vice versa. This is concept drift, and it represents a genuinely deeper, more serious problem than data drift alone.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: Concept drift is generally the more dangerous of the two, since a model experiencing concept drift can continue producing confident-looking predictions that are actually wrong in a genuinely new, previously unseen way.

blocks.text: 5. Statistical Tests for Detecting Drift

This connects back to the statistical foundations covered early in this course. The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test compares two distributions' shapes directly, producing a statistic that quantifies how different a live feature's distribution is from its training-time counterpart.

The Population Stability Index condenses that comparison into a single, easily interpretable summary score for how much a distribution has shifted overall, covered in depth in the next section. The Chi-squared test serves the equivalent role specifically for categorical features, comparing observed category frequencies against their expected, training-time frequencies.
6. Interpreting a Population Stability Index Score

blocks.alt: Interpreting a Population Stability Index Score
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444503136-369145738.png

A Population Stability Index score below 0.1 generally indicates no significant shift has occurred, and no action is needed. A score between 0.1 and 0.25 indicates a moderate shift that is genuinely worth investigating further, even if it does not yet demand immediate action.

A score above 0.25 indicates a significant shift, a real, actionable warning sign that the feature's distribution has changed meaningfully enough to warrant a closer look, and very possibly some concrete response, exactly the subject of the closing section of this topic.

blocks.text: 7. The Drift Detection Flow
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444503137-988747159.png

A scheduled drift-detection job typically runs on some regular cadence, daily for instance, pulling a recent window of live production data to examine. It compares each feature's distribution in that window against the stored training-time distribution, computing a drift score per feature using one of the statistical tests already covered.

When any feature's score crosses its defined threshold, the system flags it and alerts the team, feeding directly into the exact same alerting flow already covered in the Monitoring topic. When no feature crosses its threshold, the result is simply logged, and the system continues operating as normal until the next scheduled check.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running drift detection on a schedule rather than continuously in real time is standard practice, since meaningful distribution shifts almost always develop gradually over days or weeks, not within a single request.

blocks.text: 8. What to Do Once Drift Is Confirmed

blocks.alt: What to Do Once Drift Is Confirmed
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444503137-71952545.png

Once genuine drift is confirmed, the correct response depends directly on which kind was detected, the exact distinction covered earlier in this topic. Pure data drift, with the underlying relationship itself unchanged, is often safe to keep serving through, though it is still worth monitoring model health closely in case the situation evolves further.

Confirmed concept drift is a different matter entirely: the model's learned relationship is now genuinely stale, and retraining is truly needed to bring the model back in line with how the world actually behaves now. This leads directly into Retraining Strategies, the very next topic in this module, the standard, concrete response to a confirmed case of concept drift.
9. Worked Example
The example below computes a Population Stability Index score comparing a live data batch against a training reference distribution, using the interpretation bands covered earlier in this topic.

code.content:
import numpy as np

def population_stability_index(reference, live, bins=10):
    breakpoints = np.percentile(reference, np.linspace(0, 100, bins + 1))
    breakpoints[0], breakpoints[-1] = -np.inf, np.inf

    ref_counts, _ = np.histogram(reference, bins=breakpoints)
    live_counts, _ = np.histogram(live, bins=breakpoints)

    ref_pct = ref_counts / len(reference) + 1e-6
    live_pct = live_counts / len(live) + 1e-6

    psi = np.sum((live_pct - ref_pct) * np.log(live_pct / ref_pct))
    return psi

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
training_distribution = rng.normal(loc=1800, scale=400, size=5000)  # e.g. square footage
stable_live_batch = rng.normal(loc=1820, scale=410, size=2000)
shifted_live_batch = rng.normal(loc=2400, scale=500, size=2000)

for label, batch in [("Stable batch", stable_live_batch), ("Shifted batch", shifted_live_batch)]:
    score = population_stability_index(training_distribution, batch)
    if score < 0.1:
        verdict = "no significant shift"
    elif score < 0.25:
        verdict = "moderate shift, worth investigating"
    else:
        verdict = "significant shift, actionable warning"
    print(f"{label}: PSI = {score:.4f} ({verdict})")

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: This example checks a single feature in isolation. A real production drift-detection system runs this same kind of check across every important feature, and often across the model's output distribution too, not just its inputs.

blocks.text: 10. Key Takeaways

items: Drift Detection formalizes Monitoring's informal data health check into a rigorous statistical comparison.
Data drift changes the input distribution while the true underlying relationship stays the same.
Concept drift changes the actual relationship between inputs and the target itself, generally the more dangerous case.
The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, Population Stability Index, and Chi-squared test formally quantify distribution shift.
A Population Stability Index below 0.1 is fine, 0.1 to 0.25 is worth investigating, above 0.25 is a significant warning.
A scheduled job compares recent live data against training-time distributions, flagging features that cross their threshold.
Data drift alone is often safe to keep serving through; confirmed concept drift genuinely requires retraining.
A flagged drift score feeds into the same alerting flow already covered in the Monitoring topic.
Next up: Retraining Strategies, the concrete response once drift or degraded performance has been confirmed.
